newsitem.title: UK: Sears confirms in Freemans talks.
newsitem.headline: Sears confirms in Freemans talks.

text.p: Sears Plc, the sprawling British retail empire, confirmed on Monday that it was in "preliminary exploratory" talks with a variety of parties about selling its mail-order firm Freemans, Britain's third largest catalogue retail group, or setting up a joint venture.
"If there is an opportunity for Sears to sell Freemans or collaborate with a third party, then clearly it is something we will actively consider," said chief executive Liam Strong.
The company, which owns flagship London department store Selfridges, declined to identify discussion partners, saying it was bound by confidentiality agreements.

But the Sunday Times said private retailing and pools group Littlewoods was in "advanced" talks with Sears to buy Freemans for between 350-400 million pounds. German mail-order group Otto Versand was also tipped as a keen potential buyer.
"Unless other mail-order groups are prepared to outbid Littlewoods, a sale may be concluded before Christmas," the newspaper said.

Sears says that it was trying to establish the optimum position for its subsidiary, stating that consolidation in the mature 7.0 billion pound mail-order market would benefit all parties -- customers, suppliers and industry participants.

"We are committed to pursuing opportunities that enable us to enhance shareholder value and drive the group's strategy of concentrating on a small number of powerful brands which have the ability to achieve significant growth within the Sears Group," Strong said.
Sears, which bought Freemans for 477 million pounds in 1988, has been under pressure to boost profits -- especially since posting a steep fall in first half earnings in September.

One analyst, who declined to be named, said that Sears was looking to cut its losses with a sale, although such a move was bound to interest a number of bigger mail-order operators in the UK and abroad, which were keen on winning Freemans' substantial market share.

He said Freemans, whose profits dropped 5.5 percent to 13 million pounds in the first half of the year, may need working capital injected into it. This could limit the price bidders are willing to pay -- although larger players would be able to strip out some costs, he said.
